title: Earth surface imagery — how the layers work
intro_sentence: Zoom from the whole Earth down to a launch pad and you are looking at five layers of imagery, from satellites and from aircraft, stacked on top of each other and swapped in as you get closer.
narrative_101: No single picture can show you both the whole Earth and a launch tower. A view of the full globe resolves about ten kilometres per pixel; a photograph sharp enough to show the tower covers only a few hundred metres. So the map keeps several layers, each sharper and smaller than the one below, and shows whichever one fits the view, the same idea every online map uses.

Think of it as a stack of slices hovering one above the other. The bottom slice is one image of the whole planet. Each slice above covers less ground in more detail. At the very top you are standing on the pad, looking at a photograph taken on the ground.

Earth is the best-photographed world there is. [Landsat](app:/fleet?id=landsat) has imaged it from orbit since 1972; Europe's [Sentinel](app:/fleet?id=sentinel-copernicus) satellites have added free, open pictures every few days since 2015; and closest in, aircraft fly over whole countries to photograph them at a fraction of a metre. On the Moon and Mars the sharpest layers come from orbit, see [Moon surface imagery](planets/moon-surface-imagery) and [Mars surface imagery](planets/mars-surface-imagery); on Earth they come from aeroplanes.
body_paragraphs: Level 0 is the globe: a 4096-pixel global texture wrapped around the sphere. Earth's equator is about 40,000 km long, so each pixel spans roughly 10 km — enough for continents, deserts and ice caps, not for a single launch site. Level 1 is the context layer: around the pad you have selected, a 400 km piece of a cloud-free mosaic is draped over the globe at its true latitude and longitude, about 100 m per pixel. The layer is drawn at true scale and fades softly into the globe at its edges; its broad brightness is matched to the globe so the two meet without a seam.

Level 2 is the regional view, 16 km of ground around the pad at 10 m per pixel. Both this layer and the one below it come from Sentinel-2, a pair of European satellites (a third joined in 2024) in a [sun-synchronous orbit](orbits/sun-synchronous) that photograph a strip 290 km wide in 13 colour bands and pass over every place every five days. A single picture is often half cloud, so the company EOX builds a cloudless mosaic: from many passes over a chosen season it picks the clearest pixels for every spot, so clouds and their shadows drop out. The layers here use its 2025 edition.

Level 3 is the detail view, the pad itself. Where open aerial photography exists, it is aircraft imagery: in the United States the National Agriculture Imagery Program, which re-photographs the country at least every three years at 0.6 m per pixel or better; in Japan the Geospatial Information Authority's seamless map built from aerial photographs; in New Zealand a 2024 coastal survey by Land Information New Zealand at 10 cm per pixel, used here for [Rocket Lab's Launch Complex 1](app:/fleet?id=rocket-lab-lc-1). Where the app has no open sub-metre source, the detail view is a 2.56 km crop of the same 10 m cloud-free mosaic: softer, but always the real place. Level 4 is the panorama: a photograph taken on the ground, at the six pads where an openly licensed one exists.

How the layers meet. Each layer sits a hair above the one below, so the sharper image always wins where both exist, and each fades in by camera distance rather than popping in. At middle zooms the regional and detail patches are drawn larger than their true size so that you can see them at all; the imagery card says so. Zoom in further and the view switches to a flat patch at true scale. The imagery card in the corner always names the source, the resolution and the licence of every layer on screen, and links to it.

How the pictures reach you. What your browser downloads are copies sized for the layer, and the larger layers come in several sizes so your device's quality setting can pick one: a phone on a slow connection gets a small one, a desktop on the cinematic setting the largest. The licences differ by source: the US aerial photographs are public domain, the New Zealand survey is CC BY 4.0, and the cloudless mosaic is free for non-commercial use — which this project is.
diagram_caption: Earth's five layers of imagery, from the whole-globe texture at the base to a photograph taken on the pad at the top, with the source, resolution and ground covered by each.
